children.text: About
1 hour

by road up the mountains from Dumaguete, this is a rainforest reserve with two volcanic lakes separated by a narrow ridge. It is a cool half-day destination where you can take a boat or kayak from the landing, look down on both lakes together from the viewing tower, and enjoy Olayan Falls and birdwatching.
Balinsasayao Twin Lakes Natural Park is a protected area of about 8,016 hectares (ha) spanning the three municipalities of Sibulan, San Jose, and Valencia in Negros Oriental. It lies about
west of central Dumaguete in a straight line, or about
1 hour
up the mountain by road, and the lakes sit at an elevation of about

. The two lakes that give the park its name are volcanic crater lakes lying side by side, separated by a single narrow ridge. The larger and more accessible Lake Balinsasayao covers about 76 ha, while Lake Danao, hidden deeper in the forest, covers about 28~30 ha and sits slightly lower. Both lakes lie in a caldera basin ringed by peaks such as Mount Magahong, Mount Kalbasan, Mount Balinsasayao, and the Gintabon dome. Sources disagree on the lake depth, ranging from
to
, so the exact figure has not been confirmed.

"Balinsasayao" comes from "balinsasayaw," the Cebuano word for the swiftlet (a bird resembling a swallow), and "Danao" comes from "danaw," the Cebuano word for lake. After slash-and-burn farming and illegal logging shrank the forest here, the area became a natural park under Presidential Proclamation No. 414 on
November 21, 2000
, and in
it was named an ASEAN Heritage Park. At the marker unveiling ceremony held in Sibulan on
November 21, 2025

, it was introduced as the first in the Visayas and the 59th ASEAN Heritage Park overall. A park manager has reportedly said there are only five forest rangers to protect more than 8,000 ha of forest, so following the rules as a visitor is itself a form of protection.
Even when coastal Dumaguete tops 30 degrees at midday, it stays cool here. A
Silliman University study recorded an average annual temperature of about
around the lakes, about

lower than in central Dumaguete, with rainfall more than 2.5 times that of Dumaguete. In the early morning, mist rises over the lakes, and in the afternoon clouds slide down the mountainsides and wrap the whole lake. The lakes have no outflowing stream, so the water seeps out underground, and the lakes and surrounding forest serve as the source of rivers in southern Negros Oriental. This is also why swimming in the lakes is prohibited.

The park is one of the best places for people who come to see birds and plants. The ASEAN Centre for Biodiversity recorded 325 species of ferns, 237 species of trees, and 209 species of birds, 14 of which are globally threatened. Rare animals found only on Negros and nearby islands, such as the Negros bleeding-heart, the Visayan wrinkled hornbill, the Visayan spotted deer, and the Visayan warty pig, survive in this forest. Rather than overwhelming scenery or thrilling activities, it is a place to rest quietly in the forest and on the water, which suits travelers who want to climb to the cool mountains for a day between beach plans, families who enjoy boating and light trekking, and nature lovers who like birds and plants.

From the viewing deck next to the parking lot, you get a full view of the larger Lake Balinsasayao. You can rest over coffee or a meal at the restaurant attached to the deck, so even older visitors who find it hard to go down to the landing can enjoy the lake scenery. From the deck to the landing is a steep stone-paved path that takes about
5 minutes
on foot.
You can rent a rowboat at the landing. The fee is about
per hour, and one boat holds 4~7 people, so splitting it among your group keeps the cost low. If you want to paddle yourself, rent a kayak (about
per hour). In the calm morning, the forest is mirrored perfectly on the water. Check on-site whether kayaks are available for rent.

blocks.title: Lakeside trek to the viewing tower

children.text: It takes about
30 minutes

on foot from the landing to the viewing tower along a lakeside forest trail, and less if you cross by boat. From the top of the tower you can see both Lake Balinsasayao and Lake Danao, and from the base of the tower it is about
5 minutes
on foot to the shore of Lake Danao. The tower is also a good spot for birdwatching.

blocks.title: The submerged forest of Lake Kabalin-an

children.text: This is a small swamp lake along the road up to the lakes. Half-submerged trees reflected on the mirror-like surface make for great photos together with the early morning mist. You can stop the car on the way up, or hop off your habal-habal briefly, to visit.

blocks.title: Olayan Falls and the shallow pool

children.text: After crossing the lake by boat or kayak, or going around the lakeshore, walk about
10 minutes

more along a forest trail to reach Olayan Falls. Water tumbles in tiers over the rocks, and you can get in the shallow pool below to rest. Unlike the lakes, the falls pool is said to be open for wading, so check with the staff when you enter.

The park lies within an Important Bird Area, and in the early morning birdsong can be heard all over the forest. Fruit doves, sunbirds, and hornbills are worth looking out for. Binocular rental is about
, a guide is about
for 2~3 people, and an owl-spotting guide is about

At the fern nursery inside the park you can see edible ferns being grown, and the restaurant serves these ferns as a salad. Because the forest has 325 recorded species of ferns, you can also see large tree ferns, orchids, and pitcher plants even along the roadside.
Nipa-roofed huts are scattered around the park, which are good for eating a packed lunch, and camping is reportedly possible as well. According to a
May 2026
report, a tent rental for 3 people costs about
, and the overnight fee is about
per person. However, there are also notices saying overnight stays are not allowed without a permit, so inquire at the park office first.

The park closes at
5 PM
, and on many afternoons clouds cover the lake, so it is safest to see the Twin Lakes first in the morning and visit Casaroro Falls in the afternoon.
Cebu Pacific and PAL Express fly from Manila to Dumaguete (Sibulan Airport, DGT), taking about
1 hour 20 minutes to 1 hour 30 minutes
. From Cebu there are small Cebgo aircraft, but flights are few. The airport is in Sibulan, about
3km
north of central Dumaguete, so you can also head straight from the airport to the mountain road. Flight schedules change often, so check when you book.
From Cebu City, OceanJet fast ferries go to Dumaguete Port via Tagbilaran, Bohol, taking about
4~6 hours
including the stopover. From Tagbilaran to Dumaguete takes about
2 hours

, with around 3 trips a day. Fares range from ₱1,200 to ₱2,600 depending on the source, and timetables change by date, so check the shipping line's notices before booking. From Dumaguete Port, travel into town by tricycle.
The easiest way is to hire a vehicle or van with a driver in Dumaguete. One way takes about
1 hour
, and a full-day charter costs around
; if you add Casaroro Falls, negotiate it within the same day rate. If you drive yourself, a rental car costs about
per day and a motorbike about
per day. The road is mostly paved, but the later stretch has steep slopes and narrow winding curves, and vehicles cannot go past the souvenir shop in front of the entrance.

Budget travelers take a jeepney, multicab, or bus bound for San Jose or Amlan from near the Dumaguete public market or the Ceres terminal and get off at the Twin Lakes junction (Laraan Junction). It takes about
20~30 minutes
and costs about
, though some reviews say it took up to
1 hour
. From the junction, you ride a habal-habal (motorcycle taxi) about
30~45 minutes
up the mountain road, and drivers often ask about
one way, or about

round trip including waiting time. Choose a San Jose tourist habal-habal driver accredited by the DENR or the local government, and agree on the price and waiting time before you get on. On the way back, come down by early afternoon at the latest so it is easier to catch a jeepney at the junction.
Regular tricycles often refuse to climb the steep sections. For the mountain stretch, it is more realistic to use a habal-habal or a chartered vehicle.
Register your name and pay the entrance fee at the entrance information center. Vehicles can only go as far as the parking lot in front of the souvenir shop.
The viewing deck and restaurant are close to the parking lot, and from the deck to the lakeside landing is about
5 minutes
along a stone path.
Walking from the landing to the viewing tower takes about
30 minutes
, and from the tower to the shore of Lake Danao about
5 minutes
The Twin Lakes are in a mountainous area, so it rains much more often and is cooler than on the coast. During the dry season from
January
to
May
, the skies are clear and the mountain road is dry, making travel and trekking easy.
March to May
in particular is the best time, when you can enjoy cool air here while the coast is sweltering.
From
June
to
October

, the rainiest months in the Dumaguete area continue, and in the mountains afternoon rain and mist come almost every day. After heavy rain, parts of the mountain road may be slippery or have rockfalls, and during typhoon season there can be road washouts and closures, so check the weather forecast and the park office's notices before visiting. Regardless of the season, mornings are the most reliable, and after
2 PM
clouds often cover the lake. The average annual temperature near the lakes is about
, so you will need a light jacket in the early morning.

children.text: Prices are approximate as of
and may vary depending on local conditions.
The Twin Lakes are a day-trip destination, so it is common to stay in central Dumaguete. There are many hotels and guesthouses around Rizal Boulevard and Silliman University at roughly
per night, and if you want somewhere quiet, there are also small resorts at the foot of the mountains in Sibulan or Valencia (roughly
per night). There are notices that camping and simple lodging are available inside the park, but operations change often, so check with the park office in advance.

The restaurant and cafe at the viewing deck serve meals, coffee, hot chocolate (tsokolate), and Barako coffee, and the signature dish is the salad of edible ferns grown in the park. The menu is simple and there is no large restaurant inside the park, so it is best to bring water and snacks. Back in Dumaguete, have dinner at the restaurants along the waterfront promenade and try the city's famous desserts, silvanas and sans rival.
There is no ATM inside the park, so prepare small bills in cash for the entrance fee, boat, food, and habal-habal fares. Larger bills may not get change.
Mobile signal weakens the higher you go, so agree on a return time with your habal-habal driver in advance and, if possible, get the driver's phone number. The park has free Wi-Fi, but it is weak.
It is cool and rainy often, so bring a light windbreaker or raincoat, spare socks, and shoes with good grip.
The back seat of a habal-habal shakes a lot on steep sections, so ask for a helmet and avoid big bags.
If you arrive between
, you can get both the mist and reflection photos and avoid the weekend afternoon tour groups.
When boating or kayaking, put your phone in a waterproof pouch and do not leave cameras that are not waterproof near the water.
If you are interested in birdwatching, bring binoculars (rental about ₱200) and a telephoto lens, and walk the forest trail slowly and quietly.
Entrance fees, activity fees, and camping rules can change, so before you leave, ask the park's Facebook page or the local government tourism office for the latest information.

Swimming is prohibited in both lakes, and drones cannot be flown either. The lakes are part of the drinking water source for the Dumaguete area, and the park is a protected zone for wild birds. There was even a case where a drone was attacked by a bird. Always wear a life jacket when boating or kayaking.

After rain, the forest trails and the wooden deck at the landing are very slippery, so wear shoes with good grip instead of sandals. The stone path down from the deck to the landing is covered in moss.
Inside the natural park, collecting plants and animals, feeding wildlife, littering, and loud music are prohibited. Take all your trash back with you, and follow the signs on the forest trails.
When heavy rain or a typhoon is forecast, there is a risk of rockfalls and road washouts on the mountain road, so postpone your visit.
Operating hours are usually
8 AM to 5 PM
, and entrance fees, activity fees, and whether camping is allowed may change under park regulations, so check the latest notices. You must come down the mountain before sunset.
The Twin Lakes are in the volcanic zone of Mount Talinis (Cuernos de Negros) to the south, a different place from Kanlaon Volcano to the north (about
120km
away), which has continued erupting since
. As of a
July 2026
report, Kanlaon is at PHIVOLCS Alert Level 2 and has almost no direct effect on this area, but if there is news of a major eruption, check PHIVOLCS and flight notices.
About
1 hour
by car. The starting city for a Twin Lakes trip, with its waterfront promenade, university district, and silvanas shops.
About
40 minutes to 1 hour
by car from the Twin Lakes. A slender waterfall at the end of a stairway trail in a gorge, easy to combine into a full-day itinerary.
About
30 minutes
by car south of Dumaguete. A coastal town known for its black sand beaches and muck diving.
About
40~60 minutes
by car to Malatapay port, then about
30~45 minutes
by boat. A famous spot for snorkeling with sea turtles.
About
45 minutes to 1 hour
by fast ferry from Dumaguete. An island with waterfalls and quiet beaches.
